summary: This best current practice gives guidelines for making Interactive Connectivity Establishment finish faster in multihomed and IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack setups where some paths are broken. The guidelines are backward compatible with the original ICE specification in RFC 5245.

eli5.summary: If some of your roads are broken, try several at once rather than waiting at each. This helps video calls connect faster.

questions: how to speed up ice in dual-stack
how does ice handle ipv4 and ipv6
what is local preference in ice
subtitle: How to order ICE connectivity checks so a broken IPv6, IPv4 or interface path does not stall call setup.

tldr.problem: ICE tries candidate pairs in priority order. When IPv6 is preferred, all IPv6 checks run before any IPv4 check starts, so a broken IPv6 path causes user-noticeable delay. Unreliable interfaces can cause the same problem.
tldr.mechanism: Choose the local preference in the ICE priority formula so IPv4 and IPv6 candidates are intermingled, and give candidates from interfaces known to be unreliable a low priority.
tldr.outcome: Connectivity checks reach a working path sooner, and the change stays compatible with the original ICE specification because only priority values change.

facts.label: Example
facts.value: 2 IPv4 and 6 IPv6 addresses: IPv4 after 4 IPv6

today: RFC 8421 is a Best Current Practice published in July 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 8445 and the text says it is backward compatible with RFC 5245.

sections.title: Why Check Order Matters
sections.content:
In a multihomed host (one with several interfaces) or an IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack host, ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment, RFC 8445) benefits from a fair spread of its connectivity checks across the available interfaces and address types. A fair spread avoids long delays when one network path is broken or slow.

Following the address selection rules of RFC 6724 puts IPv6 ahead of IPv4 for the same candidate type. Checks for candidates of the same type (host, reflexive or relay) are therefore sent so that one address family is completely depleted before the other starts. If the preferred family's path is broken, setup is delayed in a way the user notices.

The RFC says this approach also supports dual-stack deployment, because users no longer have an incentive to disable IPv6. The cost is a small penalty for the address type that would otherwise have been first. Specific rules for tracking connectivity problems are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If you always try all the red doors before any blue door, and the red doors are all locked, you waste a lot of time. This document says to mix red and blue doors.

sections.title: Multihomed Recommendations
sections.content:
A multihomed ICE agent can send and receive checks on every interface and IP address, and one interface can have several addresses. It is useful to prioritize interfaces and addresses that the agent knows give stable connectivity.

The knowledge can come from simple metrics such as earlier connection success and failure rates. It can also come from a static model based on interface types such as wired, wireless, cellular, virtual and tunneled. Gathering such metrics may need permissions from the operating system.

Candidates from an interface known to be unreliable should get a low candidate priority. What counts as unreliable is implementation specific, because ICE is not limited to Voice over IP. If the application cannot learn interface types or store metrics, it should treat every interface as reliable so all of them get a fair chance. The RFC calls all of this purely an optimization.
sections.eli5: If you know one bike path is bumpy, try it last. If you do not know anything about the paths, treat them all the same and give each a turn.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Recommendations
sections.content:
Candidates should be ordered so that a run of candidates from one address family is broken up by candidates from the other. For example, an IPv4 candidate should always appear after a small run of IPv6 candidates. That makes ICE checks respond better when one address family's path is broken.

An agent may use any algorithm that gives a fair mix. It should not edit the checklist directly, because that can leave the local and remote checklists uncoordinated and make ICE slower or even fail. The recommended way is to set the local preference in the candidate priority formula of RFC 8445.

Implementations should still put some IPv6 candidates first, so IPv6 checks are likely to finish first. This follows the intent of Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305), although ICE's own pacing of checks overrules the timing recommendations in that RFC.

A simple head-start formula is Hi = (N_4 + N_6) / N_4, where N_4 is the number of IPv4 addresses and N_6 the number of IPv6 addresses. With two IPv4 and six IPv6 addresses, an IPv4 address is inserted after four IPv6 addresses.
sections.eli5: Imagine two lines of kids waiting for a slide. Let a few from one line go, then one from the other, so neither line waits forever.

sections.title: Compatibility and Priority Values
sections.content:
The candidate priority formula is priority = (2^24)*(type preference) + (2^8)*(local preference) + (2^0)*(256 - component ID). Instead of a fixed local preference for IPv4 and IPv6, the value can be chosen dynamically so the two families interleave within a candidate type. It can also be lowered for addresses from unreliable interfaces. Because RFC 8445 requires the local preference to be unique among same-type candidates for a component and stream, each value must stay distinct.

The preference can also be changed so the families interleave regardless of candidate type. This helps when many IPv6 host candidates would otherwise block checks for IPv4 server reflexive candidates. Candidates from unreliable interfaces go at the end of the checklist and are not intermingled.

The component ID part of the formula is not changed, which keeps the RTP and RTCP components close together. What matters is the order of candidates with component ID 1, which are tested first. A success unfreezes other pairs with the same foundation.

Each agent may use a different algorithm. The pair priority is 2^32*MIN(G,D) + 2*MAX(G,D) + (G>D?1:0), where G comes from the controlling agent and D from the controlled agent. Sorting by this value gives an identical checklist on both sides, so the lists stay synchronized. The agent that promoted IPv4 more cautiously, with lower IPv4 priorities, influences the list most. Depending on the nomination method, the chosen pair may change.
sections.eli5: Both players follow the same scoring rule for each pair, so even if they like different orders, they end up with the same list to work through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8445 still apply. This document only changes recommended values and shows how an agent can choose them safely.

There is one new concern. When an agent prioritizes interfaces using what it knows about the network, that choice can leak information to the remote agent. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: If you pick your order based on secrets about your roads, the other side might guess those secrets. Be careful what your choices give away.
